title: How do dogs perceive time?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether dogs perceive time, opening with a Paris court case where a dog named Scooby barked at an alleged murderer about two and a half years after an incident. They distinguish circadian oscillators (body clocks tied to roughly a 24-hour day) from episodic memory (remembering past experiences) and semantic memory (facts and skills learned without recalling when). They discuss whether a dog's anticipation of feeding time reflects episodic or semantic memory. They cover animal cognition researcher William Roberts, who concluded animals are "stuck in time" living in the present, citing pigeon and primate memory experiments, squirrel food caching, and a banana-choice experiment. The hosts argue alternative explanations exist, such as hunter-gatherer societies not storing food and primates never needing to take more bananas. They also discuss goldfish memory myths and "speciesism" in judging animal emotion and consciousness. The episode ends with listener mail ("Muppet mail") about the Muppets, Jim Henson's University of Maryland connection, a wedding at the Henson sound stage, and Ralph the Dog.
topics: Paris dog witness Scooby murder case

segments.title: Intro and Paris dog witness story
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic and recounts how a Paris court used a dog named Scooby, who barked at an alleged perpetrator in a murder-or-suicide hearing about two and a half years after the incident.

segments.title: Time, circadian oscillators, and dog feeding
segments.summary: The hosts define time as a human construct versus past, present and future, and explain circadian oscillators tied to roughly a 24-hour cycle. They discuss whether dogs anticipate feeding times through circadian rhythms or memory.

segments.title: Episodic vs. semantic memory
segments.summary: Josh explains semantic memory (facts and skills, such as learning chess, without recalling when) versus episodic memory (recalling specific past experiences, such as details of breakfast), and ties the frontal lobe to episodic memory.

segments.title: William Roberts and the 'stuck in time' theory
segments.summary: Roberts, an animal cognition researcher, tested pigeons and primates on sequence memory and concluded animals are stuck in the present without episodic memory. The hosts counter with squirrel food hoarding and the banana-choice experiment, offering alternative explanations such as lack of storage needs in hunter-gatherer societies.

segments.title: Goldfish memory and speciesism
segments.summary: The hosts question the goldfish eight-second memory claim and argue that Roberts's view is speciesist, noting that testing limits do not prove animals lack consciousness or emotion.

segments.title: Wrap-up of dog time question
segments.summary: Josh summarizes that Roberts concluded dogs do not perceive time and live in the present, and that the hosts disagree with that conclusion; he suggests searching the HowStuffWorks site for more.

segments.title: Muppet mail
segments.summary: Listener mail about the Muppets: a correction about the Children's Television Workshop, a note that Jim Henson studied at the University of Maryland, a critique comparing Sesame Street characters to special needs care, a wedding at the Henson sound stage, and a fact that Ralph the Dog has not been used since Henson's death.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks inviting listener mail and pointing to HowStuffWorks for more content.
